text: In what year was the Human Rights Act passed?
explanation: The Human Rights Act was passed in 1998 and came into force in October 2000, incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.

text: What did the Human Rights Act 1998 incorporate into UK law?

options.text: The United Nations Charter
The European Convention on Human Rights
The EU General Data Protection Regulation
The Geneva Convention

explanation: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) into UK domestic law, allowing people to enforce their Convention rights in UK courts.

text: Which Article of the Human Rights Act is most relevant to computing and privacy?

options.text: Article 2 — Right to Life
Article 8 — Right to Respect for Private and Family Life
Article 10 — Freedom of Expression
Article 6 — Right to a Fair Trial

explanation: Article 8 — the Right to Respect for Private and Family Life — is most relevant to computing, covering privacy of communications, data and personal information.

text: What does Article 8 of the Human Rights Act protect?

options.text: The right to vote in elections
The right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence
Freedom from torture and inhuman treatment
The right to a fair trial

explanation: Article 8 protects the right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence — relevant to email monitoring, data collection and surveillance.

text: Which Article protects freedom of expression including online speech?

options.text: Article 5
Article 8
Article 10
Article 14

explanation: Article 10 protects freedom of expression — including the right to share opinions online. However this right can be limited to protect the rights of others or for national security.

text: Are Human Rights Act rights absolute?

options.text: Yes — all rights are absolute and cannot be limited under any circumstances
No — some rights can be limited by public authorities in specific circumstances such as national security or public safety
Only Article 8 rights can be limited
Rights are absolute for individuals but not for organisations

explanation: Some rights are qualified rather than absolute — they can be limited by public authorities in specific circumstances such as national security, public safety or the protection of others' rights.

text: Who is primarily bound by the Human Rights Act?

options.text: All private individuals and businesses
Public authorities such as government departments, police and local councils
Only large multinational corporations
Only organisations with over 250 employees

explanation: The Human Rights Act primarily binds public authorities — such as government departments, police, courts and local councils — who must act compatibly with Convention rights.

text: How does the Human Rights Act interact with employee monitoring in the workplace?

options.text: Employers can monitor employees in any way they wish
Article 8 means employees have a reasonable expectation of privacy — excessive monitoring may breach their rights
Monitoring is only allowed with written consent from each employee
The Human Rights Act does not apply to employment situations

explanation: Article 8 gives employees a reasonable expectation of privacy. Excessive or unjustified monitoring of emails, internet use or communications may breach their right to private life.

text: How does the Human Rights Act relate to RIPA 2000?

options.text: They are entirely separate and have no connection
RIPA provides the legal framework for surveillance that must comply with Article 8 of the Human Rights Act
The Human Rights Act replaced RIPA
RIPA overrides the Human Rights Act in all cases

explanation: RIPA provides the legal framework for lawful surveillance that must comply with Article 8 of the Human Rights Act — surveillance must be proportionate and necessary to be lawful.

text: What does Article 10 freedom of expression mean for IT professionals?

options.text: IT professionals can publish any content online without restriction
People have the right to share information and opinions online, but this can be limited to protect others or prevent harm
Software code is not covered by freedom of expression
Companies must allow employees to express any opinion on work systems

explanation: Article 10 protects the right to share information and opinions online, but this is a qualified right — it can be limited to protect others' reputations, prevent harm or for national security.

text: What is the significance of the Human Rights Act for data protection in the UK?

options.text: It replaced the Data Protection Act entirely
Article 8 underpins the right to privacy that data protection law is built upon
It only applies to government data, not private companies
It has no connection to data protection

explanation: Article 8's right to privacy underpins UK data protection law — the right to have personal data handled with respect and not misused flows from the fundamental right to private life.

text: Can a UK court award damages for a breach of Human Rights Act rights?

options.text: No — the Human Rights Act only allows courts to make declarations
Yes — UK courts can award damages where a public authority has breached Convention rights
Only the European Court of Human Rights can award damages
Only criminal courts can deal with human rights breaches

explanation: Since the Human Rights Act incorporated the ECHR into UK law, domestic courts can award damages where a public authority has acted incompatibly with Convention rights.

text: A government agency wants to monitor a citizen's private emails. Which Article of the Human Rights Act is most relevant?

options.text: Article 6 — Right to a Fair Trial
Article 8 — Right to Respect for Private and Family Life
Article 2 — Right to Life
Article 5 — Right to Liberty

explanation: Article 8 protects the right to respect for private correspondence — monitoring someone's private emails without justification would engage Article 8 rights.

text: What does proportionality mean in the context of the Human Rights Act?

options.text: All citizens must be treated exactly the same
Any interference with a right must be no more than is necessary to achieve the legitimate aim
Punishments must be proportional to the crime committed
Government spending must be proportional to population size

explanation: Proportionality means any interference with a right must be no more than is necessary to achieve a legitimate aim — for example surveillance must be targeted, not blanket monitoring of everyone.

text: What right under the Human Rights Act is relevant to an employee being dismissed for posting on social media?

options.text: Article 2 — Right to Life
Article 10 — Freedom of Expression
Article 3 — Freedom from Torture
Article 12 — Right to Marry

explanation: Article 10 Freedom of Expression is relevant — employees have a right to express opinions, though this is balanced against the employer's legitimate interests and reputational concerns.
